title: The reserve that failed

facts.text: The only German reserve behind the Romanian Third Army on 19 November 1942 was XXXXVIII Panzer Corps, under Lieutenant General Ferdinand Heim, Paulus's former chief of staff.
On paper it had three armored divisions: the 14th Panzer, the 22nd Panzer and the Romanian 1st Armored. Between them they had fewer than 100 serviceable modern tanks.
The 22nd Panzer Division had little more than 30 working tanks, mostly Czech built Panzer 38(t)s, and was so short of fuel it had to borrow from the Romanians.

Parked for weeks without fuel, its tanks had become shelter for field mice, which reportedly gnawed through the insulation on the electric cables. Many tanks would not start, and no spare wiring was at hand.
On the morning of 19 November the corps was moving toward Kletskaya when orders relayed from Hitler turned it north toward Bolshoy, to Heim's fury.
The Romanian division was split off while already on the move, lost its only radio link with Heim, and the two halves of the corps never joined up.

In darkness and snow, 22nd Panzer ran into the T-34s of the Soviet 1st Tank Corps. Its tanks, with narrow tracks and failing electrics, slid on black ice. The division fell back, was surrounded, and was soon down to about a company of tanks.
Ordered to hold, Heim instead broke out to the west across the Chir River with what was left of his corps.
Hitler made him a scapegoat. Heim was recalled to Germany, stripped of his rank and jailed without trial.
The 22nd Panzer Division never recovered and was disbanded in the spring of 1943.

sources.title: Antony Beevor, Stalingrad: The Fateful Siege 1942 to 1943 (Viking, 1998), chapters 14 and 15
Earl F. Ziemke and Magna E. Bauer, Moscow to Stalingrad: Decision in the East, Chapter XXII, US Army Center of Military History (HyperWar transcription)
22nd Panzer Division, Wikipedia (citing Samuel W. Mitcham, The Panzer Legions, 2000, p. 165, and Beevor)

photoNote: German infantry move through wreckage in Stalingrad, autumn 1942. German Army propaganda company photo by PK Heine, captioned only "Stalingrad PK Heine". NARA 242-GAV-18B (naId 315834401), captured German records, Unrestricted, public domain. Cropped from the album page (label and border removed), saved 1920 x 1349. Not the Don steppe and not 22nd Panzer: it shows the Sixth Army in the city in the weeks before Uranus, so caption it as Stalingrad, autumn 1942. No captured German photo of 22nd Panzer or of tanks on the Don in November 1942 was found in NARA's 242 series (the two unindexed 242 GAV albums hold about 200 photos without captions). Neutral framing: soldiers seen from behind amid debris, no heroic pose. Alternative: 242-GAV-18A (naId 221952029), close portrait of a tired German NCO in Stalingrad, but his Iron Cross dominates the frame.
photoCredit: German soldiers among wreckage in Stalingrad, autumn 1942. German Army photo, NARA 242-GAV-18B, public domain.

declassified.fact: Heim was later brought back and given command of the German garrison at Boulogne, France, under orders to hold it to the last. He surrendered the port to the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division on 23 September 1944 and spent the rest of the war as a prisoner in Britain.

body:
Many of the tanks would not start. Field mice, sheltering in them for weeks, had reportedly gnawed through the wiring.

19 November 1942. As the Soviet offensive broke into the Romanian Third Army, the only German reserve behind it was XXXXVIII Panzer Corps under Lt. Gen. Ferdinand Heim. On paper it had three armored divisions. Together they had fewer than 100 serviceable modern tanks. The 22nd Panzer had little more than 30, mostly Czech built, and had borrowed fuel from the Romanians.

Orders relayed from Hitler turned the corps north while it was on the move. In snow and darkness the 22nd met T-34s, its narrow tracked tanks sliding on black ice. Heim broke out instead of holding, and Hitler had him stripped of his rank and jailed without trial.
